Revised read using Beige Book, FSR, and SLOOS: The FOMC’s March 20, 2019 “patient” pause is consistent with Beige Book reports of still-strong labor markets—employment increased across districts, with widespread worker shortages in IT, manufacturing, trucking, restaurants, and construction—and continued wage gains for both low- and high-skill roles alongside broader non-wage compensation. However, activity moderated early in the year: consumer spending was softer in January–February, in part reflecting harsh winter weather and higher credit costs, with mixed retail and autos; real estate cooled; and manufacturing cited weaker global demand, tariff/trade-policy uncertainty, and lingering January shutdown effects. The January 2019 SLOOS points to modest tightening in bank credit—tighter standards in C&I and CRE, wider loan spreads, and weaker loan demand across business categories and several household segments (including residential real estate and HELOCs)—with banks expecting further tightening and noting collateral-value concerns. The Financial Stability Report flags elevated business leverage, stretched valuations, and compressed risk premiums that could widen if growth slows, though funding risks remain moderate. Balance-sheet reinvestments and IOER within the floor system continue to anchor money-market control and keep longer yields supportive. Netting these, the outlook shifts from slightly positive to neutral-to-slightly negative, with downside risks incrementally higher due to tighter credit and softer demand, while labor-market strength persists and supports the “patient” stance.
